title: Your story across the portfolio
summary_easy: Ready to say answers for the questions that are about Tanay rather than about one project: tell me about yourself in three lengths for three kinds of role, walk me through your resume, which projects to lead with, what connects the work, and the full set of behavioral stories, each built from real projects with the numbers checked against the source.
summary_deep: The deck holds nine 'tell me about yourself' scripts (30 seconds, 90 seconds and 3 minutes for ML or AI engineer, data scientist, and data or analytics engineer and analyst framings) and a chronological resume walkthrough, each with keypoints for self grading. Case cards give the three lead projects per role family with a table of what each proves, its headline number and comparator, and the first follow up to expect. Five thread cards (measuring instead of trusting, replications, streaming, evals and safety, messy definitions) give spoken versions of what connects the portfolio. Behavioral cards cover the standard prompts, from most challenging project to biggest weakness, each with a story skeleton, a full STAR breakdown with labelled Situation, Task, Action and Result and evidence quotes for every number, and a 60 to 90 second spoken version. Stories draw on Dr. GRPO, distributed ViT, JMA Wireless, BEIR, Project Mark, Groundwork, Gravity Spy, the tool dependency graph, earthquake statistics, space weather, The Perfect Lap, ZTF and the teaching assistant role. The deck closes with eight questions to ask an ML or AI startup and a closing statement.

## 4. STAR bank

**Dr. GRPO (challenge, replication, constraints).** S: paper claims two GRPO biases inflate wrong answer length. T: paired replication on free GPUs. A: two flags differ; 16 questions x 8 samples per step shared by both arms; gradient tests; logprob agreement within 0.004 nats; vLLM throughput tripled; LoRA rank 64 because free GPUs have 15 GB. R: 51.6% vs 51.2% [-3.4, +4.0]; +99 tokens per step [77, 123]; wrong 680 vs 545; correct 262 vs 399 under GRPO; 55 of 500 truncated per arm; 4.35 GPU hours; not reproduced here.

**Distributed ViT (systems challenge, mistake, wrong prediction).** 1.96x at 98% fp32; 1.15x at 57% fp16; synthetic 1.92x at 96%; cpu_cores: 4; workers 2 to 8 worse (3,996 vs 4,073); dashboard 1.11x vs matched 1.15x; gate found five claims; predicted 1.8x, measured 1.96x; FSDP 2,884 vs DDP 4,376 img/s.

**JMA (proudest, stakeholders, leadership, deadline, prioritisation, process, client).** Two lines, functions with different meanings; definition interviews; sponsor approved five KPIs; 31 GB to under 5 MB; 97.3% uptime vs 46.3% attainment; manual line at 139.7%; Pugh matrix three of six; target reset to about 1,150 a week with a ramp of about 200; standup pilot 4 h to 25 min, familiarity 2.4 to 4.1; ~$355K projected pending JMA Finance; culture metric without baseline; no pipeline tests; Control Plan with named owner.

**BEIR (proudest technical, bug).** DPR 0.260 vs 0.318; TAS-B exact; title only 0.261 vs 0.260; max_seq_length = 100; 512 tokens matches; NFCorpus 38.2 vs SciFact 1.1 judged documents per query; 6 of 6, 4 exact; 12 minutes on a laptop.

**Project Mark (failure).** Eight response bar; OULAD; r = 0.56; pass rate 0.3 to 91.9 percent across quintiles; intensity collapses once days are controlled; decoys; cleared determinism checks; models solved it.

**Groundwork (data changed my mind, guardrail bugs).** BM25 recall@5 0.921 vs hybrid 0.853; monotonic improvement as dense was down weighted; classifier fired on 100% of clean passages; 0.444 under 0.5 caught 0 of 60.

**Gravity Spy (messy data, research).** 23 months; five schemas; 25,104 subjects; 8,293 channels; about 38 science accounts filtered; 49,000 spectrograms; three outputs; 455 subsystems; 0.89 AUC on 2,000 held out; ECE 0.10 to 0.05; top ten volunteers 50%; 52% consensus.

**Tool dependency graph (ambiguity, honest number).** 1,391 tools; eight assertions all failing first; four real bugs; 2,728 required, 1,770 typed, 1,768 with producers; 65 percent; 568 uncovered; slug fallback fired zero times.

**Earthquake statistics (learning fast, test not loosened).** Aki MLE with Utsu correction; Woessner and Wiemer completeness; Ogata Omori fit; p 1.1 to 1.08; [1.015, 1.070] missed b = 1; 93.7% over 300 catalogs; 16 of 20 coverage test; California 0.73 [0.66, 0.85].

**Space weather (spec was wrong).** Kp 4.67 is G1 and 5.67 is G2 in NOAA's file because NOAA rounds first; both rules tested.

**Perfect Lap (incomplete data).** 10,000 rows would shrink to 3,000; imputer recovered about 70%; imputation MAE about six laps; final test MAE 2.78 laps; team project.

**ZTF (initiative).** Closed ShopFloor's three gaps; 27,378 real alerts; 500 scored; dbt 8 models, 21 tests, 32 checks.

**TA (teaching).** 15+ labs; reproducible VMs; methodology grading; scope and authorization.

## 5. Motivation answers

- Why startups: ownership of whole systems (Groundwork, ZTF), closeness to the product decision (Groundwork's precision floor), fast feedback.
- Why this role: BEIR for retrieval, Groundwork for evals and abstention, handoff for agents; want to learn real traffic.
- Five years: trusted to say whether a model change is better; owns eval and retrieval quality; has run a service at real volume.
- Weakness: no production service at large request volume; single node gateway, Docker Compose, simulated cluster; designed for the swap; wants to learn on call and capacity work.
- Keep every motivation answer about the work and the company's product.

narration.prompt: Interviewer (ML or AI engineer role): Take your time. Tell me your story.
narration.script:
I'm Tanay, and I'm finishing an M.S. in Applied Data Science at Syracuse this December. Before that I did computer science at JSSATE Noida and a summer as a data and product analyst intern at ProProfs.

The thread through my work is that I don't trust a claim until I've measured it, including my own. It shows up in three areas.

First, retrieval. I rebuilt the central experiment from the BEIR benchmark and reproduced six of six published cells. The interesting part was the one that first disagreed: DPR on SciFact came in at 0.260 against a published 0.318. The cause was an encoder port that ships with a 100 token limit and silently cuts every abstract short. Any RAG system whose chunks are longer than its embedder's limit has the same problem. The six cells that matched taught me less than that one.

Second, evaluation and safety. Groundwork is RAG evaluation, guardrails and an LLM gateway built on SQuAD v2 and public attack corpora. Hybrid retrieval came out 6.8 points of recall worse than BM25 with my offline embedder, so I removed it. A guardrail trained on user queries fired on every clean passage, so retrieved documents now go through a pattern detector instead. I set a 60% precision floor. At that floor the system declines 96.2% of unanswerable questions. Every guardrail is also scored on an attack corpus it has never seen.

Third, training and agents. I replicated the Dr. GRPO paper on its own model, data and grader. Accuracy held and both length claims reversed, on one seed, so I report it as not reproduced here. For agents, I derived tool call order from 1,391 tool schemas, and built handoff, where every escalation has a deadline and a safe fallback. I measure systems work the same way. On a distributed training benchmark my speedup vanished in mixed precision, and one experiment showed a four core host was starving the GPUs.

Alongside that I'm a research assistant on Gravity Spy, an NSF funded project supporting LIGO. I built the ingestion pipeline over five undocumented metadata schemas, and trained a CNN whose calibration error went from 0.10 to 0.05. And I led a four person Lean Six Sigma team at JMA Wireless, which taught me how much of analytics is agreeing on definitions.

I'm looking for an ML engineering role at a startup working on retrieval, evals or agents, somewhere the team cares whether the model is actually right.
keypoints: Background in two sentences, not a life story
Thesis announced, then three signposted areas
Retrieval: the BEIR mismatch and its generalisation
Evals: three measured changes, one number each
Training and agents: reversed claims bounded by one seed
Research and leadership in one short paragraph
Ends on the role, no summary

cards.q: How should I structure 'tell me about yourself'?
cards.easy: Present, past, proof, future: what you do now, how you got here in one sentence, two or three pieces of proof with one number each, and the role you want. The proof changes with the role; the rest barely moves.
cards.deep: The answer sets the interviewer's mental model of you and decides which follow ups they ask, so the proof you choose is a choice of battlefield. Present: 'I'm finishing an M.S. in Applied Data Science at Syracuse in December, and I build retrieval and agent systems and then measure where they break.' Past: a B.Tech in computer science from JSSATE Noida and a data and product analyst internship at ProProfs, in one sentence. Future: the role and the kind of company. Length: 30 seconds on a recruiter screen, 90 seconds by default, 3 minutes only when invited ('take your time, tell me your story'). Never open with where you were born or a list of skills.

cards.q: What is the most technically challenging project you've done?
cards.easy: Dr. GRPO replication. Situation: a paper claims GRPO inflates wrong answer length. Task: test it on the paper's setup at free GPU scale with paired arms. Action: two flags differ, gradient and log probability checks, four engineering fixes. Result: accuracy held, both length claims reversed, reported as not reproduced here.
cards.deep: **Situation.** Liu et al. 2025 argue GRPO has two built in biases (a 1/|o| length normaliser and per question std scaling) and that Dr. GRPO, which removes both, stops length growth and keeps accuracy. **Task.** Rebuild the comparison on the paper's Figure 5 setup (Qwen2.5-1.5B base, R1 template, MATH questions, the authors' grader vendored unmodified) on free hardware, with the two arms paired so the comparison means something. **Action.** The two configs differ in exactly two flags. Each step samples 8 responses for each of 16 questions, the same questions in both arms. 1.5B rather than 0.5B, because the 0.5B base could not produce the strict format and GRPO had no reward to learn from. Correctness checks before results: per token gradient exactly -A/|o| against -A/budget in MLX and PyTorch, the two losses agreeing to 1e-6, merged weights reproducing LoRA outputs, sampler and learner log probabilities within 0.004 nats per step. Engineering fixes: a Metal GPU timeout from macOS paging GPU buffers, vLLM per request seeds (removing them tripled throughput), merged weights streamed one tensor at a time, bf16 keyed on compute capability. **Result.** Accuracy 51.6% against 51.2% (paired +0.4, [-3.4, +4.0]); Dr. GRPO 99 tokens longer per step [77, 123]; wrong answers 680 against 545 tokens; truncation equal at 55 of 500 per arm. One seed and 100 LoRA steps, so: not reproduced here.
cards.say: The hardest was replicating Dr. GRPO, a paper claiming GRPO makes wrong answers longer. I rebuilt it on the paper's own model, data and grader, on free Kaggle GPUs. The two arms differed in exactly two flags, and both trained on the same questions every step. The hard part was trusting the setup. I tested that the per token gradient was exactly what the paper says, and checked every step that the sampler and the learner agreed on log probabilities. Along the way I fixed a Metal GPU timeout, and found that per request sampling seeds were throttling vLLM. Removing them tripled throughput. The result: accuracy held, 51.6% against 51.2%. Both length claims came out reversed, with Dr. GRPO 99 tokens longer per step. I ruled out truncation, since each arm hit the cap equally often. It's one seed, so I report it as not reproduced here, and I'd want the paper's three seeds before saying more.

cards.q: Most technically challenging, systems version: tell me about a hard performance problem.
cards.easy: Distributed ViT. Situation: DDP scaling dropped from 98% to 57% efficiency when fp16 was enabled. Task: find the cause without guessing. Action: two named suspects, a synthetic input mode to separate them. Result: the collective scaled at 1.92x; a 4 vCPU host was starving the GPUs.
cards.deep: **Situation.** A vision transformer of 1,806,538 parameters trained on CIFAR-10 on 2x Tesla T4 with NCCL. DDP in fp32 scaled at 1.96x, 98% efficiency. The identical config in fp16 scaled at 1.15x, 57%. **Task.** Explain the drop with evidence, since hardware, model and communication volume were identical. **Action.** Correctness first: a gradient equivalence test in a real gloo process group to rtol=1e-4, shipped with an inverse test that computes the wrong thing. Matched baselines enforced by the reporting layer (a baseline differs only in rank count). Two suspects named: the NCCL all reduce and the input pipeline. Instead of tuning worker counts and reading a correlation, a synthetic input mode served pre normalised tensors from memory, removing decode, augmentation and workers. **Result.** Synthetic input scaled at 1.92x, 96%, so the collective was innocent. Real data never passed about 4,073 img/s; the artifacts record cpu_cores: 4; raising workers from 2 to 8 per rank made it worse (3,996 against 4,073). Lesson: scaling efficiency depends on the ratio of accelerator speed to host speed, and the settling measurement took six short runs and one flag.
cards.say: On my distributed ViT project, two T4s scaled at 98% efficiency in fp32. When I turned on mixed precision, the same setup dropped to 57%. Nothing else had changed: same hardware, same model, same gradient size. The tempting move was to start tuning NCCL. Instead I named two suspects, the all reduce and the input pipeline, and built one experiment to separate them. A synthetic input mode fed pre normalised tensors straight from memory, with no dataloader at all. Under that, two ranks scaled at 1.92x. So communication was fine. The run artifacts showed the host had 4 CPU cores, and adding more dataloader workers actually made it slower. The second GPU was simply going unfed. What I took from it is that speeding up the accelerator can break your scaling, because the bottleneck moves to the host.

cards.easy: Project Mark. Situation: build analytics tasks that frontier models fail fairly. Task: a deterministic, licensed, multi file product analytics trap. Lesson: decomposing a composite metric is reflexive for a capable analyst, so a fair trap must sit outside a strong reasoner's default repertoire.

Making the framing harder didn't change that. What I took away is that decomposing a composite metric is a reflex for a strong analyst, so a fair trap has to sit outside that repertoire. cards.q: Tell me about a result that did not replicate.
cards.easy: Dr. GRPO. Situation: three claims in a paper. Task: test them pairwise at free GPU scale. Action: score each claim separately, rule out truncation, credit what partly held. Result: accuracy held; both length claims reversed; reported as not reproduced here because of one seed.
cards.deep: **Situation.** Liu et al. 2025 make three claims: length grows under GRPO but not Dr. GRPO, Dr. GRPO's wrong answers are substantially shorter, and accuracy does not suffer. **Task.** Report what survives at a scale a free GPU allows, without overstating either way. **Action.** Paired comparisons throughout (same training questions, same 500 MATH500 problems), 95% bootstrap intervals. Truncation checked first: 55 of 500 final responses hit the 1024 token cap in each arm, and training truncation was similar (8.2 and 9.2 of 128 per step). Deviations tabulated (LoRA rank 64 because free GPUs have 15 GB, learning rate 5e-5, 1024 token budget, 100 steps, one seed). **Result.** Accuracy held: 51.6% against 51.2%, paired +0.4 [-3.4, +4.0]. Length reversed: Dr. GRPO 99 tokens longer per step [77, 123]; wrong answers 680 against 545; on the 199 problems both got wrong, 120 tokens longer [80, 160]. Half the mechanism appeared: GRPO's correct answers were shorter, 262 against 399. Verdict wording: not reproduced here, rather than refuted, because the bootstrap covers steps and problems, not seeds.
cards.say: I replicated the Dr. GRPO paper, which makes three claims. One held and two reversed. Accuracy held: 51.6% against 51.2% on MATH500, with a paired interval spanning zero. I'm careful about what I claim. It's one seed, and two runs with identical settings drift apart in fp16 on a GPU. So I say not reproduced here, never refuted, and I list every way my setup differs from the paper. I think that's the useful version of a replication: exact about where it disagrees, and modest about why.

cards.q: Tell me about a time you had to learn something fast.
cards.easy: Earthquake statistics. Situation: a new field (statistical seismology). Task: compute its classic statistics correctly on a live, self revising catalog. The learning method transfers: primary sources, then synthetic data with a known answer, then real data.

I implemented the maximum likelihood b-value from Aki, with Utsu's binning correction, and the Omori aftershock fit from Ogata. cards.q: Tell me about a time data changed your mind.
cards.easy: Groundwork. Situation: hybrid retrieval as the default recommendation. Task: measure all three modes on SQuAD v2. Action: ablation with exact labels; down weighting the dense side. Result: hybrid 6.8 points of recall@5 worse than BM25 with a hashing embedder; sparse became the default with a recorded flip condition.
cards.deep: **Situation.** Fusing dense and sparse retrieval is the standard recommendation, and Groundwork was built with it. **Task.** Measure retrieval on all 11,873 SQuAD v2 dev questions with exact labels (the gold passage is the paragraph the question was written from). **Action.** A three way ablation: BM25, hashing dense, and RRF hybrid. Then down weighted the dense side step by step. **Result.** BM25 reached recall@5 0.921 against hybrid's 0.853, 6.8 points better, because the hashing embedder has no semantic generalisation; fusion improved monotonically right up to the point the dense side was switched off. I didn't delete hybrid, though: all three modes still run every evaluation, and the config records the condition for flipping back, which is a real embedding model. cards.q: Tell me about working with messy, undocumented data.
cards.easy: Gravity Spy. Situation: 23 months of volunteer classifications under five undocumented metadata schemas. Task: one trustworthy dataset for modelling and science. cards.q: What is a technical opinion you hold that others might disagree with?
cards.easy: A test that cannot fail is decoration, and a timeout should never approve anything. Both are built into Tanay's code and backed by a specific bug or design.
cards.deep: **Situation.** Two opinions that show up in code. **Task.** State them with evidence rather than as slogans. **Action.** First, correctness tests need an inverse: the distributed ViT suite ships a test that deliberately computes the wrong gradient, because a correctness test that cannot fail is decoration rather than evidence; Groundwork's single pattern bug (0 of 60 attacks caught at 0.444 under 0.5) passed every multi pattern test. Second, no allow on expiry: handoff's expiry behaviours are deny, safe_fallback, escalate and hold, and a test asserts allow does not exist, because approving something nobody looked at is the absence of a decision written down as one. **Result.** Concede the cost: the second opinion means some actions do not run when they would have been fine, which is why the safe fallback exists (an unanswered failover page runs enable_read_only instead).
cards.say: One opinion is that a test that can't fail is decoration. My distributed training suite ships a second test that deliberately computes the wrong gradient, to prove the first one can catch it. I learned that the hard way in Groundwork, where every multi pattern test passed while a detector was silently off. The other opinion is that a timeout should never approve anything. In handoff, an unanswered escalation can deny, fall back, escalate or hold, and there's a test asserting that allow doesn't exist. The cost is that some safe actions won't run. That's why every risky tool declares a safer substitute, like switching a database to read only when nobody answers a failover page.

cards.q: Tell me about a time a test failed and you did not loosen it.
cards.easy: Earthquake statistics. Situation: a b-value test on a synthetic catalog with true b = 1 failed. Task: decide whether the code or the test was wrong. Action: run 300 catalogs and check coverage. Result: 93.7% coverage; the single test moved seeds and a 16 of 20 coverage test was added.
cards.deep: **Situation.** The first b-value test built a synthetic catalog with a true b of 1; the 95% bootstrap interval came out [1.015, 1.070] and missed it. **Task.** Decide whether the estimator was broken or the test was asking the wrong question, without simply widening the tolerance. **Action.** A 95% interval should miss about one time in twenty, so Tanay measured the miss rate: across 300 synthetic catalogs the interval covered the true value 93.7% of the time, close to nominal. **Result.** The estimator was fine and the single seed test was the problem. The single catalog test now uses a different seed, and a separate test requires at least 16 of 20 catalogs to cover the true value, which tests the property that matters (coverage) rather than one draw.
cards.say: On my earthquake dashboard, my first b-value test failed. I'd built a synthetic catalog with a true b of 1. The 95% interval missed it. The easy fix was widening the tolerance until it passed. But a 95% interval is supposed to miss about one time in twenty, so the real question was how often it misses. I ran it across 300 synthetic catalogs. It covered the truth 93.7% of the time, which is close to what it should. So the estimator was fine, and the test was asking the wrong question. I kept a single catalog test on a different seed, and added a test that requires at least 16 of 20 catalogs to cover the true value. That tests coverage, which is the property I actually care about.

cards.q: Tell me about working with incomplete data.
cards.easy: The Perfect Lap. Situation: pit records before 2012 were sparse. Task: avoid shrinking the dataset from 10,000 rows to 3,000. Action: a Random Forest imputer on six predictors present even in old races, validated on held out data. Result: about 70% of missing first pit laps recovered with an imputation MAE of about six laps; final test MAE 2.78 laps.
cards.deep: **Situation.** The Perfect Lap predicted the first pit stop lap from Formula 1 data (Kaggle, 1950 to 2020), filtered to post 2000 races. Pit records before 2012 were sparse. **Task.** Dropping every row with a missing pit lap would have shrunk the dataset from 10,000 rows to 3,000. **Action.** Tanay trained a dedicated Random Forest imputer on six predictors that are reliably present even in older races (driver, constructor, year, grid position, total race laps, circuit), and validated it on held out data. **Result.** It recovered roughly 70% of missing first pit laps with an imputation MAE of about six laps, tolerable because pit windows typically span ten to fifteen laps. The final Random Forest reached a test MAE of 2.78 laps. Caveat to state: imputed labels carry error into training, so the downstream MAE is partly bounded by the imputer. This was team coursework; say 'we' for the shared model comparison.
cards.say: On an F1 pit strategy project, the pit records before 2012 were sparse. Dropping every row with a missing pit lap would have shrunk the data from 10,000 rows to 3,000. So I trained a separate Random Forest just to impute the missing first pit laps. It used six features that exist even for old races, like grid position, total laps and circuit. On held out data its error was about six laps, which is tolerable when a pit window spans ten to fifteen laps. It recovered roughly 70% of the missing values. The final model, which we built as a team, predicted the first pit lap within 2.78 laps on average. The caveat I'd add is that imputed labels carry their own error into training.

cards.q: How do you think about humans in the loop for AI systems?
cards.easy: Route only the uncertain tail to people, record every correction, and design for the case where the person never answers. comms-agent covers the first two; handoff covers the third.
cards.deep: Three layers, each from a project. Confidence gating: media-pulse sends predictions below a confidence threshold to a review queue, corrections overwrite model output, and every action goes to an immutable audit log (topic accuracy 0.88 to 0.96 on a synthetic corpus; ECE 0.156 checks whether confidence is honest). Gate in the control flow: comms-agent's review gate is a conditional edge in the agent graph (9 of 24 mentions flagged, 7 corrected by a simulated reviewer before reporting). Silence as a designed case: handoff gives every escalation tiers, a deadline and a declared expiry behaviour, with no allow, and an unanswered 180 second page on an irreversible failover runs a reversible substitute. Disagreement is a second trigger: contested hypotheses raise an action's effective risk one level. Volunteers in Gravity Spy are the same pattern at scale: humans adjudicate where the model is unsure.
cards.say: I think of it in three layers. First, only the uncertain tail goes to a person. In media-pulse, low confidence predictions go to a review queue and every correction is logged. Second, the gate belongs in the agent's control flow, which is how comms-agent routes flagged items to review before anything is reported. Third, and most often skipped, is what happens when nobody answers. In handoff every escalation has a deadline, and an unanswered page on an irreversible action runs a safer, reversible substitute instead of waiting forever or going ahead.
